Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston. U.S. officials are pushing for another
round of Ukraine peace talks that would include European representatives. Envoy Steve Whitcoff
and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Philodomir Zelensky in Dublin yesterday,
following talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow. NPR's Charles Maines reports Russia's position
on Europe's role remains far from clear. Well, in his public comments, Putin wasn't
particularly receptive. He accused Europe of prolonging the war through its military support
for Kiev. He categorically ruled out this idea of European peacekeepers on the ground to help
guarantee a future security in Ukraine, saying Russia would regard these soldiers as legitimate
military targets. Whitcoff later said Putin had agreed to include Europeans in the future talks.
This is what the U.S. was after. NPR's Charles Maines reporting. The U.S. soldier arrested
in the United Kingdom on suspicion of espionage is an Army Lieutenant Colonel. NPR's Quill
Lawrence reports he was caught in a sting by British authorities. The 41-year-old Army Lieutenant
Colonel, currently being held by U.K. Metropolitan Police, has served nearly 20 years and had
deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan. A U.S. Army counterintelligence command spokesman confirms
to NPR that the suspect was caught in a sting, where he didn't know he was speaking to British
agents. U.K. authorities allege he was attempting to share sensitive information with Russia.
He's currently being held in London and will be charged early next week and then transferred to
American custody and charged under the Uniform Code of Military Justice. In recent weeks, U.S.
bases in the U.K. have been on high alert for possible attacks linked to the war in Iran.
But British authorities say this case is not related. Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
More than 100 newly elected lawmakers came to Washington to see this week for freshman
orientation. NPR's Barbara Spunt reports they'll learn everything from parliamentary procedure
to how to build a team. Freshman orientation, often called Congress school, is 10 days long.
The newly elected have a long list of things to learn. Joe Morelli is the top Democrat on the
committee that runs orientation and likely the next chairman. Setting up a congressional office,
first of all, is like its own small business. Each of them is different. They have to do their own
hiring. They have to make decisions on what the scope of each of their staff members is going to
be. They have to think about legislative procedure. Coming to Congress means life changes, too. The
incoming freshmen are figuring out their living situation come January. Some say they'll bunk with
other freshmen. Barbara Spunt, NPR News. Microsoft says it's making progress restoring service
disrupted by a worldwide outage. The company says repairs are complete in parts of the Asia
Pacific region, with efforts now expanding to other areas. Access to email is improving,
and delayed messages are being processed. You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
Former NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang is facing pressure to appear before Congress over concerns about the
tech company's ties to China. Three House committee chairs have requested a closed-door
interview on December 1st and threatened a subpoena if he refuses. Lawmakers want answers
about whether NVIDIA's advanced chips reached China in violation of U.S. export restrictions.
A new study from the federal government shows that kids in some states are not prepared for
kindergarten. NPR's Janaki Mehta reports on the findings. Kindergarten is the entryway to public
school. But not all kids enter with the skills they need to succeed, including social and emotional
development, language acquisition, and motor skills. The Government Accountability Office,
an independent watchdog, looked at data from Connecticut, Florida, Kentucky, Maryland,
and Ohio to see how prepared its youngest were for kindergarten. It found that fewer than half
of students in all those states were ready. White, Asian, or students in lower poverty areas had
better odds of being prepared. And districts with more children who had been to preschool
were also more likely to have students that came in ready for kindergarten.
Janaki Mehta, NPR News. International health experts are reviewing whether the United States
and Mexico should lose their measles elimination status. The Pan American Health Organization is
examining genetic evidence this week to determine whether the virus has been spreading continuously.
